summary.text: The Catalan recurrence gives geometric decay of the reciprocals (from index 4 onward by a factor at most \(1/3\)); together with the first few exact values, this shows that every reciprocal exceeds the entire subsequent tail, so differing starting indices strictly order the sums, while for a common start positivity strictly orders them by endpoint. The sole admissible sum not in \((0,1)\) is the exceptional value \(1\), whose fractional part is \(0\); all others lie in \((0,1)\), where taking fractional parts changes nothing.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
\]
be the Catalan numbers, and put
\[
b_n:=\frac1{C_n}>0.
\]
For integers \(j\le k\), write
\[
S(j,k):=\sum_{i=j}^k b_i.
\]
We prove that for all pairs \((j,k)\) satisfying
\[
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k,
\]
the fractional parts of the numbers \(S(j,k)\) are pairwise distinct.

The proof rests on the fact that each reciprocal Catalan number dominates the entire finite tail following it.

First, the standard quotient formula for consecutive Catalan numbers is
\[
C_{n+1}=\frac{2(2n+1)}{n+2}C_n.
\]
Indeed, directly from the defining formula,
\[
\frac{C_{n+1}}{C_n}
=
\frac{\frac1{n+2}\binom{2n+2}{n+1}}
     {\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}}
=
\frac{n+1}{n+2}\cdot
\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{(n+1)^2}
=
\frac{2(2n+1)}{n+2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}=\frac{n+2}{2(2n+1)}.
\]
If \(n\ge4\), then
\[
\frac{n+2}{2(2n+1)}\le\frac13,
\]
because this inequality is equivalent to
\(3n+6\le4n+2\), or \(n\ge4\). Thus
\[
b_{n+1}\le \frac13 b_n\qquad(n\ge4). \tag{1}
\]

It follows that, whenever \(n\ge4\), every finite tail beginning at \(n+1\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=n+1}^k b_i\le \frac12 b_n, \tag{2}
\]
where the sum is understood as zero if \(k<n+1\). To see this, repeated application of (1) gives
\[
b_{n+r}\le 3^{-r}b_n\qquad(r\ge1).
\]
Hence, for any finite endpoint \(k\ge n+1\),
\[
\sum_{i=n+1}^k b_i
\le b_n\sum_{r=1}^{k-n}3^{-r}
\le b_n\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}3^{-r}
=\frac12b_n.
\]
Equivalently, this estimate may be obtained without invoking an infinite series by induction on the length of the finite tail: after separating its first term, the remaining tail is at most one half of that first term, so the whole tail is at most
\((1+\frac12)b_{n+1}\le\frac32\cdot\frac13b_n=\frac12b_n\).

We now extend this to every \(n\ge1\), with a strict inequality:
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \sum_{i=n+1}^k b_i<b_n\quad\text{for every }n\ge1.} \tag{3}
\]
For \(n\ge4\), (2), together with \(b_n>0\), gives
\[
\sum_{i=n+1}^k b_i\le\frac12b_n<b_n.
\]
It remains to check \(n=1,2,3\). The first Catalan numbers are
\[
C_1=1,\qquad C_2=2,\qquad C_3=5,\qquad C_4=14,
\]
so
\[
b_1=1,
\qquad b_2=\frac12,
\qquad b_3=\frac15,
\qquad b_4=\frac1{14}.
\]
Applying (2) with \(n=4\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=5}^k b_i\le\frac12b_4=\frac1{28}.
\]
All terms are positive, so if one of the displayed initial terms lies beyond the endpoint \(k\), adding it only enlarges the upper bound. Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=2}^k b_i
\le b_2+b_3+b_4+\sum_{i=5}^k b_i
\le \frac12+\frac15+\frac1{14}+\frac1{28}
=\frac{113}{140}<1=b_1.
\]
Likewise,
\[
\sum_{i=3}^k b_i
\le \frac15+\frac1{14}+\frac1{28}
=\frac{43}{140}<\frac12=b_2,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=4}^k b_i
\le \frac1{14}+\frac1{28}
=\frac3{28}<\frac15=b_3.
\]
This proves (3) in all cases.

We next show that all the interval sums with positive starting index are themselves distinct. Suppose
\[
1\le j_1\le k_1,
\qquad
1\le j_2\le k_2.
\]
There are two basic comparisons.

First, if \(j_1<j_2\), then the interval \([j_2,k_2]\), if nonempty, is contained in \([j_1+1,k_2]\). Positivity of the \(b_i\), followed by (3), gives
\[
S(j_2,k_2)
\le \sum_{i=j_1+1}^{k_2}b_i
<b_{j_1}.
\]
On the other hand, because \(j_1\le k_1\), the term \(b_{j_1}\) occurs in \(S(j_1,k_1)\), and all its other terms are positive. Hence
\[
b_{j_1}\le S(j_1,k_1).
\]
Combining these inequalities yields
\[
S(j_2,k_2)<S(j_1,k_1). \tag{4}
\]
Thus a sum with an earlier starting index is always larger than every sum with a later starting index, regardless of the two endpoints.

Second, suppose the starting indices agree, say \(j_1=j_2=j\), but the endpoints differ. If, for example, \(k_1<k_2\), then
\[
S(j,k_2)=S(j,k_1)+\sum_{i=k_1+1}^{k_2}b_i.
\]
The added sum is strictly positive, so
\[
S(j,k_1)<S(j,k_2). \tag{5}
\]
The reverse inequality holds if \(k_2<k_1\).

Equations (4) and (5) show that
\[
S(j_1,k_1)=S(j_2,k_2)
\]
can hold, for positive starting indices and valid intervals, only when both \(j_1=j_2\) and \(k_1=k_2\). In other words, the map \((j,k)\mapsto S(j,k)\) is injective on all pairs with \(1\le j\le k\). Notice that this conclusion is stronger than what will be needed for the admissible pairs.

It remains to pass from the sums themselves to their fractional parts. Here the index condition is crucial. Since
\[
0<\min\{2,k\},
\]
we have \(k\ge1\). Also \(\min\{2,k\}\le j\), so in particular \(j\ge1\). There is exactly one admissible pair with \(j=1\). Indeed, if \(j=1\), then
\[
\min\{2,k\}\le1.
\]
As \(k\ge1\), this forces \(k=1\): if \(k\ge2\), the minimum would be \(2\), contradicting \(2\le1\). Thus the unique admissible pair having starting index \(1\) is
\[
(j,k)=(1,1).
\]
For this pair,
\[
S(1,1)=b_1=1,
\]
whose fractional part is \(0\).

Every other admissible pair has \(j\ge2\). For such a pair, positivity gives
\[
S(j,k)>0.
\]
Moreover, because \([j,k]\subseteq[2,k]\),
\[
S(j,k)\le \sum_{i=2}^k b_i.
\]
The tail-dominance inequality (3), applied with \(n=1\), says
\[
\sum_{i=2}^k b_i<b_1=1.
\]
Therefore every nonexceptional admissible sum lies strictly between zero and one:
\[
0<S(j,k)<1. \tag{6}
\]
Its fractional part is consequently the number itself.

We can now compare any two distinct admissible pairs \((j_1,k_1)\) and \((j_2,k_2)\).

If one pair is \((1,1)\), its sum is \(1\) and its fractional part is \(0\). The other pair is nonexceptional, so by (6) its fractional part equals its sum and is strictly positive. Their fractional parts are therefore unequal.

If neither pair is \((1,1)\), both sums lie in \((0,1)\), so both fractional parts equal the sums themselves. The interval-sum injectivity proved above shows that distinct pairs have distinct sums, and hence distinct fractional parts.

These cases exhaust all possibilities. Thus the rational numbers
\[
\sum_{i=j}^k\frac1{C_i},
\qquad
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k,
\]
have pairwise distinct fractional parts.
